case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Anton K. v. State, Department of Family & Community Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: ICWA's active-efforts duty continues even while a parent is incarcerated — incarceration affects only what efforts are possible — and the court affirmed termination after finding OCS's efforts, viewed in their entirety, were active.
key_cases.relevance: Holds that the duty to provide remedial services cannot be judicially suspended, however long the case has run.
key_cases.quote: ICWA also does not contain any provision allowing a court to approve the discontinuation of active efforts.

key_cases.case_name: Mona J. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: The superior court erred in stating that active efforts depend on a parent's willingness to engage, because the active-efforts inquiry focuses primarily on what OCS did, though the court declined to overturn precedent allowing consideration of parental non-cooperation and futility.
key_cases.relevance: Prevents a parent's non-participation from substituting for the agency's obligation to provide court-ordered services.
key_cases.quote: the active efforts inquiry depends primarily on OCS's efforts, not the parent's reaction to those efforts

key_cases.case_name: Ronald H. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: Termination of a father's rights to his Indian children, adjudicated in need of aid because of his domestic violence and aggressive behavior, was affirmed because the superior court did not err in finding OCS made active efforts.
key_cases.relevance: Applies the active-efforts review to the domestic-violence and behavioral services ordered in the case plan.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the superior court did not err in finding that active efforts were made and affirm the termination order.

key_cases.case_name: Christopher C. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights to Indian children, holding that failure to remedy and active efforts must be proved by clear and convincing evidence, that best interests is found by a preponderance, and that placement objections — including cultural ones — belong in a placement review, not the termination trial.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that the adequacy of court-ordered services is litigated as the reasonable/active efforts element.
key_cases.quote: Challenges to placement decisions, including challenges based on cultural concerns, are not properly raised in a termination proceeding.

key_cases.case_name: Simone H. v. State, Department of Health & Social Services, Office of Children's Services
key_cases.holding: The trial court acted within its discretion in refusing to release the child's therapy records to the mother for use at the termination trial, and substantial evidence supported the finding that OCS made reasonable efforts to reunify the family.
key_cases.relevance: Applies the reasonable-efforts standard to the court-ordered service package.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the trial court acted within its discretion in denying Simone's request for access to Irving's therapy records

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: ICWA section 1912(f) does not apply where the parent never had custody, section 1912(d) requires remedial efforts only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family, and section 1915(a) does not bar a non-Indian adoption when no other eligible candidate has sought to adopt; the South Carolina judgment was reversed.
key_cases.relevance: Qualifies the active-efforts propositions Alaska draws from Anton K. and Mona J. by limiting section 1912(d) to cases where termination would break up an existing Indian family.
key_cases.quote: Consistent with the statutory text, we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family’s “breakup” would be precipitated by the termination of the parent’s rights
